Android Auto Is Acting Up Again, and at This Point, I Am Too Afraid To Install New Updates
6 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Google
Yes, you’ve heard it right. Android Auto is acting up again, and this time, it also broke down the wireless connection in my car. It all happened after the installation of Android Auto 17.6, an update served through the Google Play Store as an automatic release.
Needless to say, I didn’t change anything on my side, and the configuration that worked just fine before the update is now broken after I installed the new version.
My Skoda Kodiaq is fitted with factory-installed Android Auto wired and wireless support, and I use both versions depending on where I’m going. For short drives, I rely on Android Auto wireless for the added convenience. For a longer drive, I plug in my Google Pixel 10 Pro XL because the battery impact would otherwise be significant.
However, after I installed Android Auto 17.6, neither of the two connects. I plug in my phone, and despite it starting to charge - once again, I didn’t change anything on my side, so I still use the cable that worked flawlessly before the update - Android Auto no longer fires up. I tried all the typical workarounds, including the usual cache cleaning.
After giving a try to all these fixes that don’t typically help much, I decided to remove the phone profile from the car and re-pair the mobile device with the vehicle. It worked, with Android Auto wired now launching correctly. The wireless connection was still broken, and no matter what I did, Android Auto still shut down when I removed the cable.
The next time I got in my car, boom, the same thing again. Android Auto refused to launch, and the only thing that got it up and running again was the same trick I detailed above. Needless to say, re-pairing my phone with my car every time I need to go somewhere isn’t the most convenient thing, so I started searching the web for fixes.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution It turns out I’m not the only one struggling with a similar problem. A discussion thread that was started on Google’s forums earlier this week describes a similar problem. It also happens in a Skoda (also a Kodiaq), but this time the phone involved is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The issue happens with factory Android Auto wireless.
The OP complains that Android Auto no longer works after the engine is shut down, and the only workaround is to re-pair the phone with the vehicle.
“The only fix is to forget the car on the phone (and delete the phone on the car's infotainment), then go through the whole pairing process again. After that, it works again until the next time I stop and turn the engine off,” the poster explains.
Several users stepped in and confirmed the same behavior in their cars, but someone says that Android Auto wired still works properly even when wireless is broken. This doesn’t happen in my case, as both wired and wireless appear to be unavailable when the glitch is triggered.
Oddly, one of the things I tried was a downgrade to an earlier version, but Android Auto continued to malfunction in the same way.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Other Skoda owners complain both on Google’s forums and on reddit - and it appears that owners of other cars in the Volkswagen group are struggling with a similar experience - that Android Auto is lagging and feels extremely slow after the update.
“At some point during the trip, navigation starts lagging behind, touch is very slow to react, and after some time, the whole screen gets blurry. This happens in multiple navigation software (at least Waze and Google Maps) [and] across multiple cars and different types of phones (Google Pixel, Samsung, OnePlus),” someone explains on Google’s forums.
No workaround is available in this case, despite someone explaining that updating to Android Auto 17.7 brought things back to normal.
I also installed the latest versions manually on my Google Pixel - including the recently-released Android Auto 18.0 beta - and the problems persist. The only thing that brings things back to normal is removing the phone profile and re-paring the devices from scratch every time I turn on the engine.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution At this point, I’m already afraid to install new Android Auto versions, especially when everything is working as expected. A perfectly running configuration can end up struggling with these kinds of bugs without us changing anything, so maybe Google should pay a little bit more attention to the testing phase before giving the go-ahead for production builds.
I’ve always avoided installing beta builds on my main phone, specifically because I use Android Auto as a daily driver, so stability and reliability are critical for me.
I’m still waiting for a fix, so if you somehow came across similar problems in your Skoda or Volkswagen, make sure you drop me a comment in the box below. A fix would be greatly appreciated.
